items.question: What is my educational background?
items.answer:
Rudra holds a Master of Computer Science from the University of Wollongong, Australia, completed between 2023 and 2025 with a major in Machine Learning and Big Data [[cite:2,8]]. This degree carried 96 credit points and was awarded in August 2025, supported by the UOW Postgraduate Academic Excellence Scholarship providing a 30% tuition fee waiver [[cite:8]]. Coursework included Computer Vision Algorithms and Systems, Machine Learning Algorithms and Applications, Big Data Analytics, Modern Cryptography, AI and Cybersecurity, and a double-weighted Professional Capstone Project worth 12 credit points [[cite:6]]. He graduated with High Distinctions in Programming and Data Structures, Web Development, Strategic Network Design, and the Capstone Project, along with Distinctions in Big Data Analytics, Security Essentials, AI and Cybersecurity, and System Analysis and Project Management [[cite:4]].

Prior to this, Rudra completed a Bachelor of Technology in Computer Science and Engineering with a Data Science Specialisation at Gujarat State Fertilizers and Chemicals (GSFC) University in Vadodara, India, from 2019 to 2023 [[cite:2,7]]. During this degree he received the Achiever's Award for the 2021-22 academic year [[cite:7]]. The bachelor's coursework spanned foundational mathematics, core computer science subjects such as Data Structures & Algorithms, Java, Python Programming, and Computer Networks, as well as electronics and hardware topics like Digital Electronics and Microprocessor & Interfacing, alongside industrial internships across multiple semesters [[cite:3]].

I also interned at Gurukula, Tntra Engineering from June to December 2022 as an Engineering Intern covering Full Stack and Multi-Domain work, where I built and shipped web app modules and completed multi-domain training in web development, cloud, and security [[cite:3]].

items.question: Summarize my professional profile.
items.answer:
Rudra Joshi is based in Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, and works in the software development industry [[cite:2]].

His academic background reflects a concentration in machine learning, big data, computer vision, and security, aligned with a Machine Learning and Big Data major [[cite:1]]. He completed coursework spanning computer vision, cryptography, data management, machine learning algorithms, security essentials, and AI and cybersecurity, along with a double-weighted Professional Capstone Project [[cite:5]]. On the practical side, he has built projects that demonstrate applied software development and AI engineering skills, including a retrieval-augmented generation assistant (PersonaQuery) that uses dense and sparse retrieval fusion, section-aware chunking, and Claude-based generation to answer questions grounded in personal documents [[cite:3]]. He also built a personal portfolio site using React, GSAP, and an Express-based backend, embedding the PersonaQuery assistant within it [[cite:6]], and developed JobPilot, a five-layer multi-agent system automating job application workflows with guardrails, dynamic orchestration, and model routing across agents [[cite:8]].

He has also engaged in professional development through a Forage job simulation focused on prompt and contextual engineering skills for workflow automation [[cite:4]].

Inference: Based on his coursework concentration in machine learning, big data, and security [[cite:1,5]], combined with hands-on projects in RAG systems, multi-agent orchestration, and full-stack development [[cite:3,6,8]], Rudra's professional profile suggests a strong fit for roles in AI/ML engineering, applied AI product development, and full-stack software engineering with an emphasis on intelligent systems.

items.question: What neural network architectures does the patent describe?
items.answer: The patent describes an intelligent face recognition system that combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a recurrent neural network (RNN) [[cite:5]]. The CNN and RNN together form a key generation component that uses sample facial images to produce a consistent key value for identifying a person [[cite:5]]. This architecture is also reflected in the patent's title, which explicitly references a deep recurrent neural network approach to face recognition [[cite:3]].

items.question: What is the Cognitive-Chair project about?
items.answer:
The Cognitive-Chair is an AI-based, brain-sensing wheelchair designed to assist paraplegic and quadriplegic individuals [[cite:5]]. It operates using a brain-sensing headband that reads neural signals via electro-oculography, transmits the data to a mobile application, and then relays commands to the wheelchair so it moves according to the user's neuro signal, removing the need for physical input like joysticks or manual force [[cite:4]][[cite:5]]. The research aimed to overcome common limitations of manual and powered wheelchairs, such as reliance on caregivers, upper-body strain, difficulty with curbs, high cost, and heavy weight [[cite:8]].

The project was carried out during a B.Tech degree and won the Best Paper Award at the 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Speech Technology (AIST-2022), organized by the Centre of Excellence - Artificial Intelligence [[cite:1]][[cite:5]][[cite:7]]. It was later published on IEEE Xplore, and the work also led to a related Indian patent filing for an Intelligent Face Recognition System using a Deep Recurrent Neural Network [[cite:5]][[cite:6]]. Rudra Joshi is listed as a co-author on this research alongside Kshitij Joshi, Abhilasha Vyas, Smit Joshi, and others [[cite:5]][[cite:7]].

items.question: What are the main brainwave frequencies mentioned?
items.answer: The main brainwave frequencies mentioned are Gamma, Beta, Alpha, Theta, and Delta [[cite:2]]. Beta waves are linked to focused attention on cognitive and real-world tasks [[cite:1]]. Alpha waves are associated with calm, relaxed thinking and represent the brain's default resting state [[cite:1]]. Theta waves are most common during sleep and deep meditation [[cite:1]]. Delta waves have low frequency and are associated with deep tranquility, relaxation, and dream formation during deep sleep or meditation [[cite:1]]. Gamma waves are connected to the acquisition of new information in the brain [[cite:2]].

items.question: What microcontroller is used in the wheelchair design?
items.answer: An Arduino microcontroller is used to process data received from the Android application and translate it into control signals for the wheelchair motors and other hardware [[cite:1]]. The system architecture also links the mobile application, which runs the control algorithm, to this microcontroller for managing the wheelchair's movement [[cite:2]].

items.question: Which bluetooth module does the system use?
items.answer: The system uses the HC-06 Bluetooth module for wireless transmission of signals between the headband and the microcontroller [[cite:2]]. This module functions to manage the wireless communication channel clearly and without delay, converting smartphone-transmitted data for use by the microcontroller [[cite:1]].

items.question: What is a Brain-Computer Interface according to the paper?
items.answer:
A Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), also called a Brain-Machine Interface or Direct Neural Interface, is a technology that allows users to communicate with machines or external devices using brain signals instead of the normal output pathways of peripheral nerves and muscles, giving humans the ability to control machines directly and effortlessly [[cite:1]]. It is considered one of the most promising technologies for assisting and enhancing communication and control for people with motor paralysis, such as those affected by paraplegia, quadriplegia, stroke, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, or ALS [[cite:2,7]].

A BCI system is composed of three main parts: electrodes that record electric, magnetic, or metabolic brain activity; a processing pipeline that interprets these signals, extracts relevant features, decodes patterns, and generates commands; and a computer or external device that executes those commands [[cite:5]]. BCIs are classified into invasive, non-invasive, and semi-invasive types, differing in how electrodes or sensors are placed to detect brain activity, ranging from microelectrodes inserted into the brain to sensors placed on the scalp to monitor electrical or magnetic brain signals [[cite:5]].
